Sustainable polar aprotic/poly-deep eutectic solvent systems for highly efficient dissolution of lignint Qiaoling Liu,‡ª Yang Wang,‡ª Jing Bian,ª Ming-Fei Li,ª Jun-Li Ren, ID b Xiang Hao ID *a and Feng Peng ID *a

Developing green and effective solvents is of significant importance for the utilization of lignin. Here, we demonstrated that biomass-derived polar aprotic solvents can serve as co-solvents with poly-deep eutectic solvents (PDESs) for massively dissolving various lignin samples at room temperature. The pristine PDESs were composed of polyethylene glycol derivatives and levulinic acid, while all of them exhibited poor solubility to enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), sodium lignosulfonate (LS), and organosolv lignin (OL). With the further introduction of polar aprotic solvents, including dimethylisosorbide (DMI), dihydrolevo-glucosenone (Cyrene), N-formylmorpholine (NFM), and propylene carbonate (PC), synergy between the polar aprotic solvents and PDESs dramatically increased lignin solubility to 96.82%. PC and DMI were more suitable for assisting the solubilization of EHL and OL, while Cyrene and PC were targeted at the solubilization of LS in PDESs, respectively. Moreover, a new unified co-solvent solubilization mechanism relative to the Kamlet–Taft empirical parameters was proposed. The novel polar aprotic/PDES systems provide a new avenue for boosting the high utilization of lignin.

# Introduction Lignin, a three-dimensional (3D) amorphous aromatic com- pound, is considered the second most abundant biopolymer.¹ Owing to its environmentally friendly, large-scale availability, and renewable properties, the application of lignin has attracted fast-growing attention.²,³ In general, more than 100 million tons of lignin are produced annually in pulp and paper processes, yet the large majority of lignin is burned to generate energy or discharged into waterways.⁴ The effective use of lignin provides a breakthrough pathway for its high- value utilization at scale. However, the structures of lignin are complex and irregular reticular due to the preparation methods and the origin of the resource.⁵,⁶ Thus, lignin solubi- lity in most common solvents is generally not satisfactory.

To date, much effort has been devoted to the dissolution of lignin. Several solvent systems (_e.g._, dilute acid, alkali, ammonia, and ethanol) can dissolve lignin successfully, yet their applications

However, their applications are limited by certain draw- backs, such as inherited toxicity, poor biodegradability, and high cost.10–12 Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), known as IL analogues, are synthesized by simply mixing the hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA) and hydrogen-bond donor (HBD) at a certain temperature, avoiding the use of toxic and expensive solvents.13–15 Nonetheless, the common DESs are focused on small-molecular-based com- plexes, while DESs involving polymer have little been researched. Polyethylene glycol with low cost, easy degradability, and chemical stability is regarded as a green polymer.16 A few groups have reported that polyethylene glycol with flexible alkoxy groups, such as HBA, could react with the hydrogen of hydroxyl groups in the cellulose, significantly promoting the dissolution of cellulose.17,18 Zang et al.19 further showed that a near-neutral DES (composed of choline chloride, boric acid, and polyethylene glycol-200) could separate lignin, hemicelluloses, and retain cellulose when treating wheat straw at 120 °C for 4 h. More recently, poly-deep eutectic sol- vents (PDESs) composed of polyethylene glycol derivatives, e.g., polyethylene glycol 200, 1000, poly(ethylene glycol) dimethyl ether as HBAs, carboxylic acids and amides as HBDs, were proposed by Mu et al.16,20,21 The resultant solvents could be successfully applied to dissolve both refractory metal oxides and transition metal oxides,20 which provided a new insight toward the potential application of PDESS. PDESS are usually very viscous and poorly flowable, resulting in the unsatisfactory solubilization of many polymers. Therefore, these PDESs are rarely used in lignin dissolution.

Apart from the aforementioned solvent systems, polar aprotic solvents with unique characteristics (e.g., solubilizing properties, high polarity, low boiling point, and low reactivity) have attracted much attention in a variety of areas.²²⁻²⁴ Nevertheless, the traditional polar aprotic solvents extracted from fossil lead to enormous energy consumption, environmental pollution, and present a serious hazard to human health.²¹,²³ Recently, several polar aprotic organic solvents derived from biomass have been successfully developed. For example, dihydrolevoglucosenone (Cyrene) derived from cellulose is a potential substitute for the widely used N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). Avérous et al.⁶ identified that Cyrene/H₂O formed a geminal diol structure that could efficiently dissolve various lignin samples. Alternatively, dimethylisosorbide (DMI), a nontoxic, high-boiling green solvent stemming from D-sorbitol, is considered one of the top-10 bio-based platform chemicals.²⁵ Wang and co-works indicated that DMI/H₂O can serve as a co-solvent for the treatment of Eucalyptus assisted by 72 mM H₂SO₄ at 120 °C for 60 min, in which most of the lignin and hemicelluloses could be effectively removed, and the majority of the retained cellulose was near-completely hydrolysis.²⁶ These works prompted us to determine whether these solvents could be combined with PDESS for effectively dissolving lignin at room temperature.

Herein, a series of polar aprotic/PDESs with great biocom-patibility, low cost, and low toxicity were designed by simply mixing bio-based levulinic acid (Lev) and polyethylene glycol (denoted as P-based PDESs), and poly(ethylene glycol) diacry-late (denoted as PA-based PDESs) with different molecular weights (M_w = 200, 400, and 600 Da) at room temperature, employing green multifunctional polar aprotic solvents as co-solvents derived from lignocellulose (DMI and Cyrene), non-reprotoxic N-formylmorpholine (NFM), and propylene carbon-ate (PC) (Scheme 1). The solubilization behavior of lignin in the co-sol- vents/PDESs was further analyzed, and a unified dissolution mechanism applicable to different lignin samples was proposed.

# Results and discussion ## Dissolution of lignin in different solvent systems The green PDESs were prepared by simply mixing HBA and HBD (Scheme 1) with a molar ratio of 1: 2 at room temperature for 1 h, and the detailed procedure is described in the Experimental section. For practical applications, we determined the phase-transition temperatures (Fig. S1†), viscosity, and density of the PDESs (Table S1†). It should be pointed out that the viscosity of the PDESs decreased with M_w increasing from 200 to 600.

Green polar aprotic solvent/PDESS were fabricated by mixing six PDESS (P2-Lev, P4-Lev, P6-Lev, PA2-Lev, PA4-Lev, and PA6-Lev) and four polar aprotic solvents (NFM, DMI, PC, and Cyrene) in varying volume ratios. The solubilities of lignin (EHL, OL, and LS) were further determined at room tempera- ture in the prepared solvent systems (Fig. 1–3 and Tables S4–S6†). On the contrary, the solubility of EHL in P2-Lev decreased after adding Cyrene compared to that in pure P2- Lev, indicating that Cyrene may reduce the solvating capability of the P2-Lev to act as an anti-solvent. When the Mw of the P-based PDESs was increased from 200 to 400, the EHL solubility decreased significantly (Fig. 1b and Table S2,† entry 2), yet all the polar aprotic solvents (NFM, DMI, PC, and Cyrene) in P4-Lev effectively promoted the dissolution of EHL at room temperature, regardless of the co-solvent volume ratio (Fig. 1b and Table S4†). However, when the Mw of P-based PDESS was increased to 600, the solubility of EHL slightly increased with the increase in the Mw (Fig. 1c and Table S2,† entry 3), indicating that there was no obvious correlation between the solubility of EHL and the degree of polymeriz- ation of the PDESS. Such a phenomenon differed from the case in which the lignin solubility was enhanced in the PDESS with increasing the carbon chain length.27 Besides, only PC as a co-solvent in four polar aprotic solvents contributed to the dissolution of EHL in P6-Lev with the best solubility of 25.29% (Fig. 1c and Table S4,† entry 9).

The solubility of EHL changed slightly in the PA-based PDESS, which was worse than that in the P-based PDESS (Fig. 1d-f and Table S2†). We speculated that the additional aldehyde group increased the steric hindrance between the

PDESs and lignin interaction. When PA-based PDESs with lower M_w (PA2-Lev and PA4-Lev) were combined with polar aprotic solvents, all the polar aprotic solvents showed an enhanced solubilization of EHL (Fig. 1d, e and Table S4†). However, for PA6-Lev, only PC serving as co-solvent effectively solubilized EHL (Fig. 1f and Table S4†). In general, the P-based PDESs showed better performance in the EHL solubi- lity than the PA-based PDESs. Meanwhile, the solubilization effect of EHL depended on the type and amount of PDESs and polar aprotic solvents. The solubilization effect of EHL signifi- cantly decreased when the content of co-solvents increased from 20 to 80 vol% and all the polar aprotic solvents (except 20 vol% Cyrene/P2-Lev) mixed with a lower M_w of PDESs showed an outstanding solubilization effect for EHL, yet when the M_w of the PDESs was increased, only PC contributed to the enhanced solubility of EHL.

More lignin solubility tests were performed to screen the solvating capacity of PDESs mixed with different polar aprotic solvents, and the dissolution behavior of LS was determined (Fig. 2 and Table S5†). First, the dissolution of LS in different PDESS were measured. Similar to the dissolution behavior of EHL in PDESs, there was no obvious correlation between the LS solubility and the M_w of PEG in the PDESS. P4-Lev provided the best performance in the dissolution of LS (25.52%) in the P-based PDESs at room temperature (Fig. S2 and Table S2,† entry 1). The solubility of LS in the PA-based PDESs decreased with changing PA2 to PA4, but increased for the PA6-based PDESS. PA2-Lev was one of the best PA-based PDES, with a solubility of 13.70% at room temperature for LS (Fig. S2 and Table S2,† entry 5).

Synergy was also observed between P2-Lev and the polar aprotic solvents. All the compounds could solubilize LS at room temperature after adding polar aprotic solvents to P2-Lev, and the solubilities of LS in 20 vol% NFM/DMI/PC increased from 20.94% to 78.94%, 96.82%, and 92.52%, respectively (Fig. 2a and Table S5,† entry 2). When the M_w of the P-based PDESS was changed from 200 to 400, the solubility of LS roughly decreased, but all the polar aprotic solvents still promoted the dissolution of LS at room temperature effectively, in which NFM, PC, and DMI played an obvious role. When the M_w of the P-based PDESs was increased to 600, Cyrene and PC dramatically improved the dissolution of LS. Similarly, the PA-based PDES mixed with polar aprotic solvents showed irreplaceable synergy in dissolving LS (Fig. 2d-f). PC was one of the best polar aprotic solvents as a co-solvent in PA2-Lev, with a great solubility of 52.47% (Fig. 2d and Table S2 (entry 4), Table S5, (entry 17)†). However, when the M_w was varied from 200 to 400/600, the best choice of co-solvent was Cyrene (Fig. 2e and f). All the polar aprotic solvents/PDESS could improve the solubility of LS except for NFM and DMI in P6-Lev, in which PC was the best one for the dissolution of LS.

solubilities of OL were negligible in P4-Lev and P6-Lev, suggesting that a lower _M_w was beneficial for the dissolution of OL, resulting from their lower viscosity and greater opportu- nity for hydrogen-bond formation with more HBA (Table S1†).28 In addition, the P-based PDESs showed better performance than the PA-based PDESs in the dissolution of OL. With the incorporation of co-solvents, NFM, DMI, and PC showed an excellent ability to promote lignin dissolution in P2-Lev (Fig. 3a and Table S6†). Since the optimal solvent efficiency for dissolving lignin occurs at lower co-solvent con- centrations, the solubility of OL in 20 vol% NFM/P2-Lev increased from 20.41% to 61.76% (Fig. 3a and Table S6,† entry 2), and the solubilization effect was weakened when the _M_w of the P-based PDESs increased (Fig. 3a–c). With regard to the P4- and P6-based PDESs, all the polar aprotic solvents, especially DMI and Cyrene, showed an enhanced solubilization effect for OL. All the polar aprotic solvents contributed to the dis- solution of OL, while only DMI and PC showed a dramatically increased dissolution ability for OL in the PA-based PDESs. Specifically, PC was the preferred co-solvent for efficient dissol- ving OL in PA2-Lev, while DMI was still dominant for the dis- solution of OL in all the PA-based PDESs (Fig. 3d–f).

Here, the solubilities of the three lignin samples (EHL, LS, and OL) in the P-based PDESs were superior to the PA-based PDESS. For EHL, NFM, PC, and DMI promoted the solubility of lignin, in which PC exhibited a better solubilization in higher M_w_ PDESS, especially in the PA-based PDESS. For LS, synergy between the polar aprotic solvents and PDESS was observed (except for NFM, DMI in P6-Lev). Cyrene was preferred to the solubilization in the PDESs with a higher M_w_, while PC was more suitable in lower M_w_ PDESS. For OL, all the polar aprotic solvents (except Cyrene/P2-Lev) played an obvious role in the solubilization effect for OL; in particular, the strong solvating capacity of DMI as a co-solvent made it more efficient in dissolving OL in all the PDESs.

Thus, the difficulty of dissolution was decreased, causing the relatively higher solubility of LS in the co-solvent/PDESs. In the aromatic region, signals for the S, G, and p-hydroxyphenyl (H) units were detected in the three

lignin samples, indicating that these lignin samples were derived from herbaceous plants. The obvious condensation signal of condensed S units was detected at around 103.5-106.5/6.15-6.45 ppm in the spectrum of OL, which might greatly limit the solubility of OL. In the aromatic region of LS, the chemical shifts of the G and H units changed signifi- cantly, indicating that the presence of the sulfonate groups led to a reduction in the electron cloud density of the aromatic rings. Meanwhile, the contained sulfonate groups afforded LS with much higher polarity, thus leading to the special dis- solution behavior of LS.

## Conclusions In conclusion, novel sustainable polar aprotic/PDESs were successfully prepared and applied for dissolving different types of lignin, including EHL, LS, and OL at room temperature. It was found that the lignin solubility varied with the type of co-solvents and PDESs. First, there was no correlation between the lignin solubility and the degree of polymerization of PEG oligomers in PDESs, while the influence of the terminal group of these chains could not be ignored. Specifically, the P-based PDESs showed superior performance for lignin dissolution than the PA-based PDESs. Meanwhile, NFM, PC, and DMI actively participated in the EHL dissolution process in the PDESs, with PC showing excellent EHL solubilization in the PA6-PDESs. For LS, all the co-solvents were capable of assisting in the dissolution of LS in the PDESs (except NFM, and DMI in P6-Lev), among which PC was more suitable in the P2- and P4-based PDESs, and Cyrene was more suitable for the P6-PDESs. For OL, all the polar aprotic solvents (except Cyrene/P2-Lev) played an obvious role in the solubilization effect of OL; in particular, the strong solvating capacity of DMI as a co-solvent was more efficient in dissolving OL in all the PDESs. We believe our PDES/co-solvents systems could be applied in several areas, including 3D printing, film packaging, and gel materials.

A new unified solubilization mechanism was proposed by the Kamlet–Taft parameters. Co-solvent/PDESs with π* > the critical values showed excellent performance for the different lignin samples (EHL, OL, and LS) due to the dispersion forces of lignin and the interactions with the aromatic parts of lignin. The critical values depend on the degree of polymerization of the solvent and the type of lignin. **Preparation of the all-green polar aprotic solvents-based** **solvent systems** The PDESs were synthesized based on a previous report with some modifications.57,58 First, the desired HBAs (P2, P4, P6, PA2, PA4, and PA6) and levulinic acid (LA) were mixed at a molar ratio of 2:1, 1:1, or 1:2. Second, the mixture was stirred at room temperature on a magnetic stirrer for 30 min. Finally, the desired PDESs were obtained after the above liquid was heated at 60 °C for 24 h under vacuum to remove the con- tained water. Subsequently, the all-green solvents were pre- pared by mixing the PDESs with different volume fractions of polar aprotic solvents and then stirring for 30 min.

Here, we demonstrated that biomass-derived polar aprotic solvents can serve as co-solvents with poly-deep eutectic solvents (PDESs) for massively dissolving various lignin samples at room temperature. The pristine PDESs were composed of polyethylene glycol derivatives and levulinic acid, while all of them exhibited poor solubility to enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), sodium lignosulfonate (LS), and organosolv lignin (OL). With the further introduction of polar aprotic solvents, including dimethylisosorbide (DMI), dihydrolevo-glucosenone (Cyrene), N-formylmorpholine (NFM), and propylene carbonate (PC), synergy between the polar aprotic solvents and PDESs dramatically increased lignin solubility to 96.82%. PC and DMI were more suitable for assisting the solubilization of EHL and OL, while Cyrene and PC were targeted at the solubilization of LS in PDESs, respectively. Moreover, a new unified co-solvent solubilization mechanism relative to the Kamlet–Taft empirical parameters was proposed. The novel polar aprotic/PDES systems provide a new avenue for boosting the high utilization of lignin. # Introduction Lignin, a three-dimensional (3D) amorphous aromatic com- pound, is considered the second most abundant biopolymer.¹ Owing to its environmentally friendly, large-scale availability, and renewable properties, the application of lignin has attracted fast-growing attention.²,³ In general, more than 100 million tons of lignin are produced annually in pulp and paper processes, yet the large majority of lignin is burned to generate energy or discharged into waterways.⁴ The effective use of lignin provides a breakthrough pathway for its high- value utilization at scale. However, the structures of lignin are complex and irregular reticular due to the preparation methods and the origin of the resource.⁵,⁶ Thus, lignin solubi- lity in most common solvents is generally not satisfactory. These results indicated that the co-solvent/PDESS contributed to the fractionation of lignocellulose. ## Conclusions In conclusion, novel sustainable polar aprotic/PDESs were successfully prepared and applied for dissolving different types of lignin, including EHL, LS, and OL at room temperature. It was found that the lignin solubility varied with the type of co-solvents and PDESs. First, there was no correlation between the lignin solubility and the degree of polymerization of PEG oligomers in PDESs, while the influence of the terminal group of these chains could not be ignored. Specifically, the P-based PDESs showed superior performance for lignin dissolution than the PA-based PDESs. Meanwhile, NFM, PC, and DMI actively participated in the EHL dissolution process in the PDESs, with PC showing excellent EHL solubilization in the PA6-PDESs. For LS, all the co-solvents were capable of assisting in the dissolution of LS in the PDESs (except NFM, and DMI in P6-Lev), among which PC was more suitable in the P2- and P4-based PDESs, and Cyrene was more suitable for the P6-PDESs. For OL, all the polar aprotic solvents (except Cyrene/P2-Lev) played an obvious role in the solubilization effect of OL; in particular, the strong solvating capacity of DMI as a co-solvent was more efficient in dissolving OL in all the PDESs. We believe our PDES/co-solvents systems could be applied in several areas, including 3D printing, film packaging, and gel materials. A new unified solubilization mechanism was proposed by the Kamlet–Taft parameters. Co-solvent/PDESs with π* > the critical values showed excellent performance for the different lignin samples (EHL, OL, and LS) due to the dispersion forces of lignin and the interactions with the aromatic parts of lignin. The critical values depend on the degree of polymerization of the solvent and the type of lignin. These results indicated that the co-solvent/PDESS contributed to the fractionation of lignocellulose. ## Conclusions In conclusion, novel sustainable polar aprotic/PDESs were successfully prepared and applied for dissolving different types of lignin, including EHL, LS, and OL at room temperature. It was found that the lignin solubility varied with the type of co-solvents and PDESs. First, there was no correlation between the lignin solubility and the degree of polymerization of PEG oligomers in PDESs, while the influence of the terminal group of these chains could not be ignored. Specifically, the P-based PDESs showed superior performance for lignin dissolution than the PA-based PDESs. Meanwhile, NFM, PC, and DMI actively participated in the EHL dissolution process in the PDESs, with PC showing excellent EHL solubilization in the PA6-PDESs. For LS, all the co-solvents were capable of assisting in the dissolution of LS in the PDESs (except NFM, and DMI in P6-Lev), among which PC was more suitable in the P2- and P4-based PDESs, and Cyrene was more suitable for the P6-PDESs. For OL, all the polar aprotic solvents (except Cyrene/P2-Lev) played an obvious role in the solubilization effect of OL; in particular, the strong solvating capacity of DMI as a co-solvent was more efficient in dissolving OL in all the PDESs. We believe our PDES/co-solvents systems could be applied in several areas, including 3D printing, film packaging, and gel materials. A new unified solubilization mechanism was proposed by the Kamlet–Taft parameters.
